title: Non-Standard Port
summary: Non-standard port describes command and control traffic that carries a protocol on a port number it would not normally use. The operator keeps the protocol, often TLS (Transport Layer Security), but changes the port, so the packet no longer matches the protocol and port pairing that many firewalls, proxies and parsers assume. The same idea appears on the victim side, where registry values or configuration files are edited so a service such as Remote Desktop listens somewhere else, which quietly changes the shape of the network. The evidence lives in firewall logs, network flow records, service configuration changes and the process that opened the socket, not in a single clear alert. A defender compares the observed pairing against the normal profile of that asset: a workstation suddenly accepting TLS on an odd port is far more interesting than a known web server doing the same thing.

beginner.definition: Every network service usually has a standard port number, like a fixed door number for that service. A non-standard port is when a service uses a different door number instead. Attackers do this to slip past filters that only watch the usual door. It can also confuse tools that expect the usual pairing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most network rules are written around port numbers. If an attacker moves traffic to an unusual port, those rules may miss it. The traffic can look like an unknown service, so nobody investigates it. Your team may also misread logs and think a web server is running somewhere strange. Watching for unusual port use closes a common blind spot.
howItWorks: Each common network service has a port number that people expect it to use.
The attacker sends that same protocol on a different port number instead.
Filtering rules that only allow the usual port may no longer match the traffic.
Analysis tools may parse the packet wrongly because the port does not fit.
On the victim host, configuration files or registry values can move a service.
Defenders see the change in firewall records, flow data and service settings.
beginner.example: Imagine an airport where visitors normally enter through the main hall. Guards watch that hall closely. A traveller who uses the staff side door may walk past everyone. The door itself is normal, but the person is not expected there. Some guards only hold a list of main hall visitors, so they see nothing strange. Careful staff compare each door against the people who normally use it.
takeaways: A port number is not proof of what a service actually does.
Learn the normal ports for each host, then question changes to them.
Check both network logs and host configuration for unusual port settings.

objectives: Define a non-standard port and explain why an attacker would use one.
Describe how a port change can defeat firewall rules and protocol parsers.
Identify the logs that reveal unusual protocol and port pairings.
Explain how host configuration can be changed to move a listening service.
Apply a baseline of normal ports to decide when an unusual port is suspicious.
